concept.name: Iron butterfly
concept.definition: An iron butterfly is a four-leg, same-expiration strategy combining a short straddle at the middle strike (short call and short put at the same strike) with a long out-of-the-money strangle as wings (long lower-strike put, long higher-strike call). Entered for a net credit, it reaches maximum profit when the underlying finishes exactly at the middle strike.
concept.intuition: It is a short straddle with wings: you sell the at-the-money call and put for a large credit, then buy cheap far-out options to cap the damage if the stock runs.
concept.mechanics: Net credit = premiums sold minus premiums bought; maximum gain is the credit at the middle strike; maximum loss is the wing width minus the credit, realized beyond either long strike. It can be decomposed into a bull put spread and a bear call spread sharing the same short strike.
concept.formula: Max gain = net credit; max loss = (K_wing - K_body) - net credit; breakevens = K_body +/- net credit.
concept.failure_modes: Maximum profit requires the underlying to pin the body strike exactly, a low-probability outcome; the large credit accompanies steep short gamma near expiration, and assignment of an ITM short leg can leave a residual stock position.
concept.misconceptions: The large credit is not an edge over the iron condor — it reflects the narrower, lower-probability profit zone; on a risk-adjusted basis neither structure has an inherent advantage.
concept.example: With XYZ at $100: sell the $100 call and $100 put, buy the $90 put and $110 call for a $5.00 net credit. Max gain $500 at exactly $100; max loss $500 at or beyond $90 or $110; breakevens at $95 and $105.
